newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom share price dip reflected company rules.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom share price dip reflected company rules.

text.p: A brief drop in the price of gas monopoly RAO Gazprom early on Monday reflected company restrictions on the shares, and the fact that there are effectively several categories of Gazprom stock, dealers said.
But Gazprom shares are likely to continue rising ahead of the international placement of its stock, they said.
Gazprom was a late $0.475 on Monday on the Russian Trading System (RTS), off an intraday high of $0.505, but above Friday's closing $0.445, continuing recent strong gains.
But early on Monday, before trade officially opened, it traded at $0.300 on the RTS.
"This deal was done before the RTS opened. Probably it was someone trading shares which have not been "refused" by Gazprom," said United City Bank dealer Yury Sychev.
Gazprom rules require shareholders who wish to sell their shares to offer them to the company first.
Gazprom has 90 days to refuse these shares. Shares refused in this way can then be sold as usual, and are usually re-registered within three days.
Gazprom shares traded on the RTS normally fall into this category.
But it is possible to trade shares without first obtaining Gazprom's permission. In that case the buyers of the shares must themselves apply to Gazprom for the "refusal".
However shares traded in this way may need two months for delivery, trading at a discount of up to 20 percent as a result, dealers said.
Such deals are normally over-the-counter, not on the RTS.
These rules mean Gazprom, one of Russia's biggest companies by market capitalisation, has some of its most illiquid shares.
Dealers said one of Gazprom's aims with the restrictions is to stop shares trading at too low a price. The company has launched regular auctions of its shares to create an orderly market.
The auctions have been held roughly once a week since March, and the price has risen steadily. At the last auction on Friday the average price was 3,010.15 roubles ($0.555).
Some dealers said a sudden dip in Gazprom on the RTS during the auction was due to concern about Gazprom's assets in a generally weaker market.

Earlier this month Gazprom's chairman Rem Vyakhirev said the government had frozen some of Gazprom's accounts to put pressure on it to pay back taxes. A company statement on Monday said no accounts or assets had in fact been frozen.
But Creditanstalt Grant dealer Andrei Galperin said the tax issue was not behind the fall.
"We don't have clients like that in Gazprom. These are not small speculators. They understand that all this will pass," he said.
But the auction price, though much higher than the RTS price, is still only a third of the price for Gazprom's forthcoming international issue of American Depositary Shares.
The managers of the issue said last week the ADS's will be priced at $14-$16 each. Each ADS is equivalent to 10 ordinary shares.
The underlying shares have risen sharply since the ADS pricing announcement, and were the strongest performer on the RTS last week, attracting much foreign investment.

"The West is willing to buy because it is hoping for those prices (announced by the managers)," said UCB's Sychev. "Personally I expect a leap in prices when they give some more information about the placement."
